content: Reactive drug administration (RDA) involves providing antimalarial medications to individuals who either live with or near a person with a confirmed malaria infection or were likely exposed to the infection at the same time and place as the index case. The goal of RDA is twofold: to treat existing infections and to prevent new infections during the post-treatment prophylaxis period of the drug. Commonly used medications include artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) or chloroquine, and in some cases, primaquine is used for radical cure of Plasmodium vivax or as a single low-dose for Plasmodium falciparum to target gametocytes. Reactive interventions should focus on the probable location of infection for the index case. This location is determined through case investigations, which use the date of symptom onset and the known incubation period of the parasite species to identify where the person was likely infected. If the likely location of infection is a residence, RDA can be administered to the household members of the confirmed case and potentially extended to neighbors. If the infection was imported from another area, RDA can be given to individuals who shared the same exposure risk, such as co-travelers or co-workers, to reduce malaria transmission. Programs implementing RDA must have the capacity to conduct thorough case investigations at the residence to identify the likely location of infection and co-exposed individuals. They should also be able to enumerate and provide antimalarial medications to people living with or near a confirmed malaria case and others sharing the same risk of infection. The individuals receiving antimalarial medications through RDA should either share the same risk of acquiring infection as the index case or be at risk of acquiring infection from the index case. This includes household members, neighbors, co-travelers, and co-workers. However, if the infection was imported and the residence is not in a receptive area, RDA may not provide any benefit. For Plasmodium vivax, programs should carefully consider how to safely and feasibly administer treatment to prevent relapses. This may involve testing for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency before administering 8-aminoquinoline drugs, ensuring effective pharmacovigilance systems, and having emergency access to blood transfusion services. WHO guidelines recommend that RDA should be one component of a broader malaria elimination program, which includes intensive follow-up of every case as outlined in the Framework for Malaria Elimination. RDA relies on a robust passive surveillance system that detects suspected cases, tests them with quality-assured parasitological methods, and investigates all cases at their residences. Without these elements, RDA is unlikely to impact malaria transmission. Determining the likely location of infection through case investigation is essential to identify where and among whom the RDA intervention should occur. If the infection is determined to have been acquired locally, RDA should be administered to other residents of the same household. Depending on local malaria epidemiology and ecology, the radius of RDA may be extended to include neighbors. If the index infection was not acquired at the residence, RDA should target all individuals identified as having the same exposure risk as the index case. These individuals are likely to include those who traveled, worked, or engaged in leisure activities with the index case. In cases where the infection was imported and the household is not in a receptive area, RDA may not provide any benefit. Countries with very low or low malaria transmission but not yet close to achieving zero indigenous cases should prioritize RDA and reactive indoor residual spraying (IRS) over reactive case detection and treatment (RACDT). However, RACDT should be added to RDA when countries are closer to elimination to enhance surveillance sensitivity, monitor progress toward elimination, and provide evidence of malaria-free status post-elimination. RDA should be implemented according to standardized operating procedures (SOPs), which include developing and verifying a household listing of all individuals within the RDA limits and identifying those who may have been co-exposed. The program should aim to provide antimalarial medication to everyone listed, using various approaches to reach all at-risk individuals. High coverage of the targeted population and good adherence to the antimalarial medication are critical for the success of RDA programs. RDA programs often require asymptomatic, healthy individuals to take medication despite not feeling ill, which may lead to adverse reactions. Improving coverage and adherence necessitates building understanding and trust in the institutions implementing the program. Community engagement is therefore a key factor in improving participation rates and adherence to the full treatment course. All eligible adults and children should receive a complete therapeutic course of antimalarial medication at doses recommended by the manufacturer. Drug dosage should be determined by weight whenever possible, with age-based dosing used only when weight is unknown. The antimalarial medications chosen for RDA should meet several criteria: they should be WHO-recommended and prequalified, effective against local parasites, different from the first-line treatment where possible, have a superior safety and tolerability profile, provide a longer duration of post-treatment prophylaxis, have a positive public reputation and acceptability, and be available at low cost. In areas with Plasmodium falciparum, programs may consider including a single low dose of primaquine in RDA to enhance its gametocytocidal effect, although there is no evidence of additional benefit from this in RDA programs. A drug regimen that can be administered as a directly observed single dose is preferred over multi-day regimens. Programs considering the use of 8-aminoquinoline drugs for the radical cure of Plasmodium vivax should ensure testing for G6PD deficiency, effective pharmacovigilance systems, and emergency access to blood transfusion services. They should also assess whether sufficient coverage and adherence to the full course of radical cure can be achieved. The systematic review identified six cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) in four sub-Saharan African countries (Eswatini, Gambia, Namibia, and Zambia) and one non-randomized study (NRS) from Peru assessing the impact of RDA. Most infections in the African cRCTs were due to Plasmodium falciparum, while the NRS in Peru primarily included Plasmodium vivax infections. The evidence suggests that RDA may reduce malaria prevalence and probably reduces the incidence of parasitemia, but it likely results in little to no difference in the incidence of clinical malaria. The certainty of evidence for these outcomes is low to moderate. Adverse events were reported in four cRCTs, with mild to moderate events being the most common. The NRS in Peru, which used chloroquine plus seven days of primaquine for radical cure of Plasmodium vivax hypnozoites, reported no adverse events, but there was no active pharmacovigilance system in place. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) judged the benefits and undesirable effects of RDA to be small, with low overall certainty of evidence. They noted that the comparator in several studies was RACDT rather than no RDA, which may have underestimated the impact of RDA. The GDG concluded that RDA is likely acceptable, feasible, and potentially cost-effective when case numbers are low enough to allow for case investigations, including in post-elimination settings working to prevent re-establishment of infection. The GDG recommended further research to assess the impact, acceptability, feasibility, and potential harms of RDA, including the safe provision of 8-aminoquinoline drugs for radical cure of Plasmodium vivax. They also highlighted the need to investigate the optimal approach to defining the target area for RDA implementation, the timing of RDA after index case detection, and whether additional rounds of RDA should be repeated in the same areas to prevent subsequent transmission.
